---
title: "Evaluating undirected cell-type networks"
---

There is **no** complete ground-truth GRN for murine gastruloids. Mouse
TF catalogues are incomplete, and undirected GGM edges are not the same
objects as directed TF–target arrows. Evaluation in the **core** is
therefore **relative**: methods against each other, against technical
resampling of this atlas, and against partial literature priors. It is
not a claim of causal recovery.

The score families and stability scenarios below are **inspired by**
GRETA [@badia-i-mompelComparisonEvaluationMethods2025] and BEELINE
[@pratapaBenchmarkingAlgorithmsGene2020]. We do not import those
pipelines. We keep three **undirected**, observational families:

1.  **Statistical robustness and distributional alignment** — does the
    fitted Gaussian (or its graph) stay put under resampling, and does
    it match the type-level law that DeCovarT needs?
2.  **Topological comparison** — skeleton similarity among the three
    core estimators, without a true DAG.
3.  **Knowledge-driven scoring** — TFs connected to plausible targets
    and pathway overlap, always as overlap with an incomplete prior.

Directed DAGs, multimodal ATAC/ChIP recovery, perturbation
forecasting, and any metric that needs a **known true skeleton** are
**perspectives** (@sec-metrics-perspectives). They judge a different
estimand than @eq-grn-estimand.

## Statistical robustness and alignment {#sec-metrics-stat}

These scores do not need a true graph. They ask whether
$(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j})$ is a
stable, distinguishable plug-in for @eq-grn-convolution.

### Resampling

With one experiment, the honest uncertainty is **conditional on this
atlas**:

-   **Technical cell bootstrap** within type, labels fixed
    (@sec-align-bootstrap). Re-estimate $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j}$; record
    edge inclusion frequencies (stability selection in the sense of
    Meinshausen and Bühlmann [@meinshausenStabilitySelection2010]) and
    the Frobenius / Bures spread of $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}$.
-   **Gene or cell downsampling** as a coverage check. GRETA found that
    TF and gene *sets* can look stable while **edges** collapse under
    downsampling — a warning we should expect for glasso supports as
    well.

The three core estimators (`huge`, `SILGGM` `D-S_GL`, `PLNnetwork`) are
**deterministic given the data and the penalty**. We do not report
seed-overlap diagnostics for them.

Biological (multi-organoid) bootstrap is **unavailable**. Reporting a
bootstrap interval as if it were between-experiment uncertainty would
repeat the pseudoreplication error of @nte-pseudoreplication.

Observation-model **contamination** (wrong sampling layer, spillover,
missing types) is not a GRN-stability experiment. It belongs to the
misspecification sweep of @sec-sensitivity.

::: {#nte-stars .callout-note}
## :information_source: StARS selects $\lambda$ from edge instability

In `huge`, StARS (stability approach to regularisation selection)
[@liuStabilityApproachRegularization2010] does
**not** score likelihood or the numerical accuracy of
$\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$. Liu, Roeder and Wasserman choose the
**least amount of regularisation** that still makes the graph sparse
and replicable under random sampling. For each penalty $\lambda$, the
data are subsampled, the graph is re-estimated, and
$\hat\pi_{gg'}(\lambda)$ is the fraction of subsamples in which edge
$\{g,g'\}$ appears. Edge instability is of the form

$$
2\hat\pi_{gg'}(\lambda)\bigl(1-\hat\pi_{gg'}(\lambda)\bigr),
$$

which is near zero when the edge is almost always absent or almost
always present, and largest when it appears about half the time. These
terms are averaged over possible edges. StARS then takes the
**least sparse** graph whose overall instability stays below
`stars.thresh`
([`huge.stars`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/huge/topics/huge.stars);
[`huge.select`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/huge/topics/huge.select)).

Practical settings:

-   `stars.thresh = 0.1` — package default; allows about 10% graph
    variability and tends to give a denser network;
-   `stars.thresh = 0.05` — stricter, typically sparser; the
    documentation presents $0.05$ as more appropriate when the
    graphical model is believed to be well specified.

The selected $\lambda$ determines **both** the adjacency
(`refit`) **and** the precision (`opt.icov`). There is no separate
StARS criterion for a “best precision matrix”. The `huge` documentation
also warns that StARS can **overselect** edges in Gaussian graphical
models, so we compare it with EBIC (@sec-grn-penalty-stability) rather
than treating it as ground truth. For `SILGGM` and `PLNnetwork` we
reuse the same instability diagnostic on technical subsamples; we do
not pretend those packages ship StARS.
:::

### Likelihood and information criteria

On the Gaussian scale actually used by the estimator,

-   **eBIC** (extended BIC) is the usual glasso selection criterion when
    FDR methods are not used;
-   held-out log-likelihood on cells left out within type (still
    technical, not biological).

These scores compare **nested Gaussian models**. They do not validate a
PLN latent graph against a glasso graph on NPN data: the observation
models differ. Cross-family comparison must move to a common object —
the exported $(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j})$ on the
**linear** DeCovarT scale — and use distributional distances.

### Distances between type-level Gaussians

Closed forms, for non-degenerate
$P_{j}=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j})$:

**Kullback–Leibler**

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{j}\parallel P_{\ell})
&=
\tfrac12\Bigl[
\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\ell}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j})
+(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot\ell}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j})^{\top}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\ell}^{-1}
(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot\ell}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j})
-G
+\ln\frac{\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\ell}}{\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}}
\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-kl-gauss}

**Jeffreys** $J(P_{j},P_{\ell})=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{j}\parallel P_{\ell})+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{\ell}\parallel P_{j})$
is the symmetric version used as a separation monitor in the feature
chapter.

**Hellinger** via Gaussian affinity, and **MixSim overlap**
$\omega_{j\ell}^{\mathrm{MS}}$ as the sum of misclassification
probabilities [@melnykovMixSimPackageSimulating2012; @R-MixSim],
are the right “can DeCovarT tell these types apart?” scores. They are
**not** graph metrics; they are metrics on the generative object. (The
superscript $\mathrm{MS}$ avoids clashing with precision entries
$\omega_{gg'}$.)

**Bures–Wasserstein** (@sec-align-ot) is a perspective metric. It splits
mean displacement from covariance geometry when an external population
Gaussian is available.

::: {#nte-metrics-scale .callout-note}
## :information_source: Compare laws on the DeCovarT scale

KL between NPN-space Gaussians is not KL between count-scale
pseudo-bulks. After each estimator has exported @eq-grn-export, compute
KL / Hellinger / $W_{2}$ / MixSim on **that** Gaussian, the one that
enters the convolution. Otherwise a “better” SILGGM graph can win on
NPN likelihood and lose as a deconvolution prior.
:::

## Topological comparison {#sec-metrics-topo}

These describe **shape and concordance**, not correctness against a
true DAG. The core object is the undirected adjacency
$A_{gg'}=\mathbf{1}\{\hat\omega_{gg'}\neq 0\}$.

-   degree distribution and a power-law diagnostic (many biological
    networks are not strictly scale-free);
-   hub overlap across types (rewiring of hubs is a DeCovarT-relevant
    summary);
-   clustering coefficient, number of connected components, modularity;
-   overlap coefficients of edge **sets** between the three methods
    (intersection over the smaller set), which avoids punishing a
    method for returning a larger graph.

**Structural distances between two estimated undirected graphs** (no
true skeleton required) follow the `bnlearn` comparison helpers
([Comparing network structures](https://www.bnlearn.com/examples/compare-dags/)):

-   `hamming()` — Hamming distance: the number of edge additions and
    deletions needed to turn one skeleton into the other (no
    orientation term, because our graphs are undirected);
-   `shd()` — structural Hamming distance (SHD). For DAGs it also
    counts reversals; on undirected skeletons it reduces to the same
    add/delete count. Report both the raw distance and a version
    normalised by $G(G-1)/2$.

Concordance between `SILGGM` and `PLNnetwork` is a **robustness**
number, not a validation. If the three core estimators disagree on
edges, that is the expected state of observational GRN inference, not a
bug unique to gastruloids. Downstream DeCovarT should therefore **not**
depend on a single edge being true; it should depend on the SPD
covariance being a stable discriminator.

Metrics that need a **known true skeleton** (precision, recall, $F$,
AUPRC, MCC against a simulator DAG) are in @sec-metrics-true-skeleton.

## Visualisations {#sec-metrics-viz}

The aim is to **compare structure and inference**, not to decorate a
methods section. Each display should answer one question. Penalty-path
and `funkyheatmap` scoreboards live in @sec-grn-penalty-path; this
section is about **supports, signs, and modules**.

**Supports and concordance (one type, one time)**

-   Binary adjacency heatmaps, genes ordered by a **common**
    hierarchical clustering (from a consensus distance
    $d_{ab}=1-\bar r_{ab}$ of methods, or from a biological
    ordering). Side-by-side heatmaps of $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{j}$
    for two types make rewiring visible; a third panel of
    $|\hat\omega^{(j)}_{gg'}-\hat\omega^{(\ell)}_{gg'}|$ is the
    differential-network view.
-   **Upset plots of edge presence** across `huge`, `SILGGM` and
    `PLNnetwork` at a fixed type $\times$ time: how many edges are
    unique to one estimator, shared by two, or shared by all three.
-   **Upset plots of edge sign**, which is stricter. An edge is a
    signed pair
    $\bigl(\{g,g'\},\operatorname{sign}(\hat\omega_{gg'})\bigr)$.
    Two methods can share the support and still disagree on the sign of
    the partial correlation; that disagreement is visible only in the
    signed Upset.
-   On-diagonal degree bars or a simple graph drawing **only** for a
    tiny TF subgraph; whole-transcriptome hairballs are not figures.

**Leiden modules from the precision weights**

Treat $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{j}$ as a weighted undirected graph
with edge weights $|\hat\omega_{gg'}|$ (or
$|\rho_{gg'\mid\mathrm{rest}}|$ from @eq-partial) on the selected
support. Cluster genes with Leiden
([`igraph::cluster_leiden()`](https://igraph.org/r/html/1.3.4/cluster_leiden.html)):
the weights enter the quality function directly, so modules reflect
**strength of conditional dependence**, not just binary adjacency.
Compare partitions across the three estimators (adjusted Rand index)
and across types (rewiring of modules). Do not feed the dense
$\check{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}$ into Leiden.

**Signed partial correlations**

-   Diverging tiles of
    $-\omega_{gg'}/\sqrt{\omega_{gg}\omega_{g'g'}}$ with a midpoint
    scale, not viridis (the latter encodes magnitude, not sign). Keep
    gene order shared across types.

**Stability**

-   Edge-inclusion frequencies from the technical bootstrap as a
    heatmap or as a reliability curve (precision among edges with
    inclusion $>t$, as $t$ varies).
-   Sankey or alluvial **only** when nodes have a natural order (time,
    lineage). For unordered type-to-type edge flow, a chord diagram is
    the usual display; we do not need one in the core stationary
    analysis.

## Knowledge-driven scoring {#sec-metrics-knowledge}

**Literature / knowledge (observational, undirected)**

-   **Marker TFs**: is a known type marker present as a hub, or as a
    high-degree node in $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{j}$ for that type?
-   **TF–target edges**: if $g$ is a TF and $g'$ a curated target,
    does the undirected edge $\{g,g'\}$ appear? Resources: CollecTRI,
    DoRothEA, and mouse TF catalogues — all incomplete.
-   **TF–TF via shared targets**: two TFs that share many neighbours
    may reflect a complex or an artefact of co-expression; report
    overlap with PPI / IntAct only as a soft score.

**Predictive (observational)**

-   How well does the graph **topology** predict held-out expression
    (gene $\sim$ neighbours)? For a GGM this is almost circular (the
    model *is* a prediction of each node given the rest), but a
    **held-out cell** nodewise $R^{2}$ is still a useful calibration:
    a graph that does not predict expression of its own nodes is a bad
    Gaussian.
-   Gene-set enrichment of Leiden or other modules (Hallmark, KEGG,
    Reactome) is a sanity check, not a causal test.

## Practical scorecard for this repository {#sec-metrics-scorecard}

For each core estimator and each cell type $j$:

1.  **Robustness:** bootstrap edge-inclusion; StARS-style instability
    (@nte-stars); $W_{2}$ / KL of $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}$
    across bootstraps.
2.  **Alignment:** KL / Hellinger / MixSim **between types**
    (discrimination) and between the type-level Gaussian and the
    empirical cell cloud (@sec-align).
3.  **Topology:** Hamming / SHD and Upset concordance among the three
    estimators; degree / hub concordance; Leiden ARI; no hairball as a
    main figure.
4.  **Knowledge:** fraction of curated TF–target pairs recovered as
    undirected edges; marker-TF degree; stated as **overlap with an
    incomplete prior**, not as accuracy.
5.  **Downstream (the score that actually matters for this project):**
    DeCovarT deconvolution error under a fixed mixture design when
    $\boldsymbol{\zeta}$ comes from each GRN method, with the misspecification
    sweep of @sec-sensitivity.

Item 5 is the only metric that is **identified** with the paper's
estimand. Items 1–4 are supporting diagnostics. Perspectives stay out
of the scorecard until the corresponding data or simulator is in
`data/processed/`.

## Perspectives {#sec-metrics-perspectives}

The core graphs are **undirected**, **observational**, and fitted
without a true gastruloid skeleton. The following tasks are useful
later; they are not gates for DeCovarT.

### When a true skeleton is available {#sec-metrics-true-skeleton}

On a simulator whose GRN we supplied (@sec-align-mc), or on a curated
Boolean skeleton used only as a **reference**, the usual ranking scores
apply to the **undirected** adjacency:

| Score | Definition on skeletons | Caveat |
|-------|-------------------------|--------|
| Precision / recall / $F_{1}$ or $F_{0.1}$ | TP, FP, FN against the reference skeleton | Needs a true or curated support; GRETA weights precision $10\times$ recall because inferred GRNs are sparse |
| Early precision | Precision among the top-$k$ edges | Robust when $k$ is the expected degree $\times G/2$ |
| AUPRC / AUROC | Ranking of edges | AUROC is too optimistic on sparse graphs; prefer AUPRC |
| Structural Hamming distance | Hamming / SHD against the true skeleton | Scale with $G$; report also normalised SHD |
| MCC | Balanced correlation of binary edges | Still needs a reference |

Without that reference, these numbers are undefined. CPDAG /
orientation metrics apply only if we leave the core and score a DAG.
We do not, in the main pipeline.

Boolean / logical models (BEELINE curated networks; BoolODE) are
mechanistic simulators: truth tables $\to$ ODEs $\to$ synthetic
counts. They supply a **known skeleton** for AUPRC when we simulate.
They are not fitted to Suppinger as the DeCovarT graph. Using a Boolean
model *as the prior* and a GGM *as the data-driven proposal* is a
legitimate consistency check; using the Boolean model *as*
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j}$ would abandon the Gaussian convolution.

### Directed DAGs {#sec-metrics-dags}

Our estimand is an undirected SPD precision. Directed causal metrics
(SHD on orientations, SID, CPDAG comparisons) judge a different
object. They belong here only if a later analysis fits a DAG.

### Orthogonal assays {#sec-metrics-omics}

ChIP-seq, CUT&RUN, and ATAC-seq (or multiome) networks are closer to
**physical interaction** than a partial correlation. They are
orthogonal, complementary modalities; they are **not** measured in the
core Suppinger scRNA-seq table we use for $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j}$. If a
later gastruloid multiome appears, GRETA is a possible evaluation
harness; SCENIC+ / CellOracle / Dictys remain out of the DeCovarT
**input**, because they return directed regulons, not SPD precisions.
The honest use is: project our undirected skeleton onto TF–CRE–gene
triples and score literature overlap; do not replace
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j}$ with a regulon adjacency.

### Perturbations and integer programmes {#sec-metrics-perturb}

We do not have a gastruloid TF knockout atlas. GRETA found that
multimodal GRNs **struggle to capture causal relationships from
perturbation assays**, even when predictive and literature scores look
decent. We therefore **do not** use TF-activity enrichment after
perturbation as a gate for DeCovarT.

**CORNETO** [@rodriguez-mierUnifyingMultisampleNetwork2025] reformulates
knowledge-driven network inference as a joint constrained optimisation
problem (LP / MILP) over prior knowledge networks. It is **not** a
GGM. As a perspective scorer, it can take our data-driven support and
ask whether a sparse subnetwork of a PKN explains the omics under flow
/ Steiner / CARNIVAL constraints. That tests **mechanistic
plausibility**, not Gaussian fit.
